READING THE LABELS

Confidence belongs to a claim.

An author identity can be plausible while its portrait is uncertain. A title can match closely while the edition differs. Each profile therefore assesses attribution, metadata, images and survival evidence separately. These labels are research judgments, not calibrated statistical probabilities.

LevelInterpretation
High confidenceStrong agreement across title, creator and year, or direct evidence such as an edition comparison, identified holding or published census. Automated metadata matches remain candidates; a high score does not verify a physical copy.
Medium confidenceSeveral details agree, such as a name, title, lifetime or year. A material detail still needs checking. Automated matches can reach this level without confirming a physical edition.
Low confidenceA useful lead: an OCR repair, initials or surname match, another edition, or a weak title/creator match. False matches are expected and remain visible for review.
Very low confidenceAn exploratory surviving-copy scenario based on tentative catalogue information and broad assumptions. It has not been calibrated against an edition census; the actual total may fall outside the range.
UnresolvedThe sources checked do not support the field yet. Unknown is preserved as a result of the search.
COPIES IN THE WORLD

Known copies. Estimated survival.

A published census establishes known copies, usually an open lower bound. A historical print run describes how many were produced. Neither automatically gives the number surviving today. Where an evidence-based range can be stated, its assumptions and confidence appear beside it; where the upper bound is unknown, the range stays open. Catalogue entries, online scans, volumes and search hits are never added together as if each represented a distinct complete physical copy.

The separate ballpark estimate layer uses assumed print runs and survival fractions to offer broader coverage. Its low and very low confidence ranges are exploratory scenarios. They do not increase the verified-edition or survival-research totals.

The research includes nearby editions as leads for images and contents. Their surviving-copy counts remain attached to those editions and are not transferred to the family’s edition.

SOURCES & LIMITS

A trail you can follow.

Author candidates combine the catalogue’s own headings with public authority records. Book candidates are ranked using normalized title wording, creator names and publication years against a broad scientific and historical corpus. OCR distortions, translated names, homonyms, reprints and short generic titles can produce false connections. Public coverage is uneven across languages and disciplines; an unmatched record is not evidence that a book or author is exceptionally rare.

Reference images show the external source’s copy. Automated thumbnails can show a cover, title page, bookplate or another page. Exact-edition galleries that have been checked are distinguished from these tentative previews. A biography describes a proposed person; it does not by itself prove that all linked works belong to that person.

The original family catalogue scans and OCR remain attached to each record. Sources and retrieval dates accompany research. The earlier main-page historical charts still use the original, explicitly labeled 1,664-card sample.
